title: Multiple Interfaces
summary: Achieve multiple inheritance of type in Java by implementing multiple interfaces, eliminating the diamond problem while creating multi-capability classes.
learningObjectives: Implement multiple interfaces in a single class using comma-separated syntax
Explain how pure contracts avoid the diamond problem of multiple class inheritance
Cast a multi-interface object between different interface reference types
Handle method signature collisions when two interfaces declare identical methods
expectedOutcomes: You can build flexible, composable classes implementing multiple interfaces
You understand how reference casting reveals different functional lenses on the same heap object

activities.title: Practical Context: Composing Multiple Capabilities Safely

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: A modern smartphone is not just a telephone. It is a High-Definition Camera, a GPS Satellite Navigator, an MP3 Music Player, and an NFC Payment Device. Each of these capabilities has an industry standard contract. You can hand your phone to a photographer who uses it strictly as a Camera. You can clip it onto your car dashboard where navigation software uses it strictly as a GPS Navigator.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: The smartphone is a single concrete class (`SmartPhone`). `Camera`, `GpsReceiver`, `AudioPlayer`, and `NfcPayer` are separate interfaces. Depending on which reference lens you view the phone through (`Camera c = phone;`), you access only that interface's specific operations.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Multiple interfaces allow a single object to fulfill multiple diverse roles across different parts of a system without inheriting conflicting state.

activities.content:
In real-world engineering, sophisticated components must fulfill multiple distinct functional roles simultaneously.

Consider a distributed storage system:
- A `CloudBlob` must support reading (`Readable`).
- It must support cryptographic verification (`Verifiable`).
- It must support serialization for network transfer (`Serializable`).

Java allows classes to implement multiple interfaces simultaneously, providing full multiple inheritance of type without architectural ambiguity.

activities.title: Multiple Interface Implementation: Definition and Collision Resolution
Multi-Capability Smart Device
activities.explanation: SmartPhone implements 3 interfaces. In main, upcasting pixel to PhoneDevice, CameraDevice, and GpsDevice exposes only the methods of that respective interface.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: Each interface specifies a single capability.
The heap contains a single `SmartPhone` object.
Casting to `PhoneDevice` restricts access to `makeCall()`, isolating callers from camera and GPS APIs.

activities.title: Shared Method Signature Across Interfaces
activities.explanation: Printable and ScreenDisplayable both declare void render(). A single implementation in CanvasDocument satisfies both interfaces without collision.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: Both interfaces declare `void render()` with identical signatures and return types.
Both `p.render()` and `s.render()` dynamically execute that single implementation.

questions.question: How does Java support multiple inheritance?
options: Through multiple class inheritance: class A extends B, C
Through multiple interface implementation: class A implements B, C
questions.explanation: Java strictly forbids multiple class inheritance, but fully supports multiple inheritance of type through interfaces.

questions.question: Why does implementing multiple interfaces avoid the Diamond Problem of multiple class inheritance?
options: Because interfaces are compiled into C++
Because traditional interfaces contain only method specifications (no instance fields or state), so there is no ambiguity regarding memory layout
Because interfaces can only have private methods
Because the JVM chooses one interface randomly
questions.explanation: The Diamond Problem in classes arises from duplicate instance state and conflicting constructor chains. Pure interfaces carry no state, eliminating collision ambiguity.

questions.question: What happens if two interfaces declare `void print()` with identical signatures, and a class implements both?
options: Compile error: duplicate method signature in interfaces
The class provides a single `public void print()` method that satisfies both interface contracts simultaneously
The compiler forces the class to rename one of the methods
questions.explanation: If two interfaces declare identical method signatures, writing one implementation satisfies both contracts cleanly.

questions.question: When does implementing two interfaces cause an unresolvable compiler error?
options: When both interfaces have more than 5 methods
When both interfaces declare a method with the same name and parameter types, but incompatible return types (e.g. int vs String)
When one interface is public and the other is package-private
questions.explanation: In Java, a class cannot have two methods with the same parameter list differing only by primitive or incompatible return types. Such a collision cannot be resolved.

questions.question: Given `class Car implements Drivable, Insurable`: What is the result of `Insurable ins = new Car(); ins.drive();`?
options: Compilation error: drive() is not declared in the Insurable interface
questions.explanation: The compiler checks member availability against the reference type (`Insurable`). Because `drive()` belongs to `Drivable`, `ins.drive()` fails compilation.

questions.question: How can you access `drive()` from `Insurable ins` in the previous question?
questions.explanation: Because the underlying object on the heap is a `Car` (which implements both interfaces), downcasting or side-casting to `(Drivable) ins` succeeds.

questions.question: What happens if two interfaces declare constants with the same name (e.g. `int TIMEOUT = 10;` and `int TIMEOUT = 20;`), and a class implements both?
options: The class compiles; referencing `TIMEOUT` unqualified is ambiguous, but accessing `InterfaceA.TIMEOUT` or `InterfaceB.TIMEOUT` resolves it cleanly
The second constant overwrites the first
questions.explanation: The class compiles without issue. Referencing `TIMEOUT` inside the class is ambiguous, but qualifying with the interface name disambiguates it.

questions.question: How many interfaces can a single Java class implement?
options: No theoretical limit (as many as memory and specification constraints permit)
questions.explanation: Java imposes no language limit on the number of interfaces a class can implement: `implements I1, I2, I3, ...`.

questions.question: Which core Java class famously implements multiple interfaces including `Serializable`, `Comparable<String>`, and `CharSequence`?
What is 'side-casting' in Java with multiple interfaces?
options: Casting an integer to a float
Casting an object from one interface reference type to another interface reference type implemented by the same underlying object
Casting a class to its superclass
questions.explanation: Side-casting (e.g., `(Camera) phoneReference`) converts between unrelated interface types implemented by the same underlying object.

interviewQA.question: Why did the designers of Java allow multiple inheritance of interfaces but forbid multiple inheritance of classes?
interviewQA.answer: Multiple class inheritance leads to the Diamond Problem: if class D extends classes B and C, which both extend class A, class D inherits duplicate copies of class A's fields, causing memory layout ambiguity and constructor collision. Interfaces (traditionally) contain only method specifications and no instance fields. Inheriting multiple specifications creates no state ambiguity, so Java permits multiple interface inheritance safely.

interviewQA.question: What is 'side-casting' in Java, and when can it throw a `ClassCastException`?
interviewQA.answer: Side-casting occurs when an object referenced by one interface type is cast to a completely unrelated interface type (e.g. `interface A` to `interface B`). The compiler permits this because the underlying concrete object *might* implement both interfaces. At runtime, the JVM checks the object's class metadata. If the object implements interface B, the cast succeeds; if not, it throws `ClassCastException`.

interviewQA.question: How do you resolve a collision where two implemented interfaces define identical constant names?
interviewQA.answer: You resolve it by explicitly qualifying the constant with the desired interface name (e.g. `InterfaceA.MAX_LIMIT` or `InterfaceB.MAX_LIMIT`). Referencing `MAX_LIMIT` unqualified inside the implementing class causes a compile-time ambiguity error.

interviewQA.question: What is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) from SOLID, and how does multiple interface adoption enable it?
interviewQA.answer: ISP states that 'clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.' Instead of one massive 'fat' interface (`Machine` with print, scan, fax, staple), architects break it down into cohesive, focused interfaces (`Printer`, `Scanner`, `Fax`). A class like `MultiFunctionPrinter` can implement all three, while a simple `LaserPrinter` implements only `Printer`, keeping clients decoupled from unused methods.

interviewQA.question: What happens if a class implements two interfaces that both declare `default` methods with identical signatures?
interviewQA.answer: This creates a default method conflict. The compiler refuses to compile the class and forces the developer to override the method explicitly in the implementing class, resolving the ambiguity (either with new logic or by delegating via `InterfaceA.super.method()`).

interviewQA.question: Can an interface extend multiple interfaces? Provide an example from the Java Standard Library.
interviewQA.answer: Yes. An interface can extend multiple interfaces using commas: `public interface SubInterface extends Super1, Super2`. A prominent JDK example is `java.util.concurrent.BlockingDeque<E>`, which extends both `java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue<E>` and `java.util.Deque<E>`.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I know the syntax for implementing multiple interfaces separated by commas.
I understand why interfaces avoid the Diamond Problem of multiple class inheritance.
I know that a single method implementation satisfies multiple interfaces with identical signatures.
I understand the collision error when two interfaces have identical signatures but different return types.
I know how to resolve constant name collisions using explicit interface qualification.
I can perform side-casting between interface references implemented by the same object.
I understand how multiple interfaces support the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP).
I know that an interface can extend multiple other interfaces using extends.
I understand how the 'lens effect' restricts callable methods based on the reference type.
I can build a composable multi-capability class fulfilling multiple business contracts.

practiceProblems.title: Multi-Role Person Implementation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Implement multiple roles on a single class:

1. Interfaces:
   - Interface Student: void study();
   - Interface TeachingAssistant: void gradeAssignments();

2. Class CollegeTutor (implements Student, TeachingAssistant):
   - Field: private String name
   - Constructor: CollegeTutor(String name)
   - Method 1: @Override public void study() printing '<name> is studying for midterm exams'
   - Method 2: @Override public void gradeAssignments() printing '<name> is grading lab assignments'

Test in Main:
CollegeTutor alex = new CollegeTutor("Alex");
alex.study(); alex.gradeAssignments();.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Alex is studying for midterm exams
Alex is grading lab assignments
hints: Use class TeachingAssistant implements Student, Teacher
Both study() and teach() must be public.
practiceProblems.description: Let a single Person class implement both Student and TeachingAssistant interfaces.

practiceProblems.title: Cloud Resource Lifecycle and Metrics
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Combine lifecycle and monitoring interfaces from scratch:

1. Interfaces:
   - Interface Lifecycle: void start(); void stop();
   - Interface Monitored: void reportMetrics();

2. Class CloudInstance (implements Lifecycle, Monitored):
   - Field: private String instanceId
   - Constructor: CloudInstance(String id)
   - Method 1: @Override public void start() printing 'Instance <id> STARTED'
   - Method 2: @Override public void stop() printing 'Instance <id> STOPPED'
   - Method 3: @Override public void reportMetrics() printing 'CPU: 42%'

Test in Main:
CloudInstance vm = new CloudInstance("i-0994bf");
vm.start(); vm.reportMetrics(); vm.stop();.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Instance i-0994bf STARTED
CPU: 42%
Instance i-0994bf STOPPED
hints: Class header: class ComputeInstance implements Lifecycle, Metrizable
practiceProblems.description: Implement Lifecycle and Monitored interfaces on a CloudInstance class from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Ambiguous Constant Reference
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Disambiguate conflicting interface constants:

Bug: Both FreightLimits and PassengerLimits define `int LIMIT = ...`. Calling `LIMIT` in Elevator creates an ambiguous reference error!

Your Task:
1. In Elevator.displaySpecs(), refer to the constants explicitly:
   - `FreightLimits.LIMIT` (500kg)
   - `PassengerLimits.LIMIT` (8 people)

Test in Main:
Elevator el = new Elevator();
el.displaySpecs();.
hints: Qualify the constants: WeightBearing.MAX_CAPACITY and PassengerCarrier.MAX_CAPACITY.
practiceProblems.description: When two interfaces define a constant with the same name, disambiguate using InterfaceName.CONSTANT.
